entries.26e0f98015ab4476b22bc792dd2c5ab1445de845: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11408"/><div sID="gen20648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11408"/><hi type="bold">15. consume thy filthiness out of thee--</hi>the object of God in scattering the Jews. <div eID="gen20648" type="x-p"/>
entries.d351a69e3fead7d961073d25b8c06fbe8cff8a17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11409"/><div sID="gen20649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11409"/><hi type="bold">16. take thine inheritance in thyself--</hi>Formerly thou wast Mine inheritance; but now, full of guilt, thou art no longer Mine, but thine own inheritance to thyself; "in the sight of the heathen," that is, even they shall see that, now that thou hast become a captive, thou art no longer owned as Mine [Vatablus]. Fairbairn and others needlessly take the Hebrew from a different root, "thou shalt be polluted by ('in,' [Henderson]) thyself," &c.; the heathen shall regard thee as a polluted thing, who hast brought thine own reproach on thyself. <div eID="gen20649" type="x-p"/>
entries.e368468224248c1f4882f519768221306451bd73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11410"/><div sID="gen20650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11410"/><hi type="bold">18. dross ... brass--</hi>Israel has become a worthless compound of the dross of silver (implying not merely corruption, but degeneracy from good to bad, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.22">Is 1:22</reference>, especially offensive) and of the baser metals. Hence the people must be thrown into the furnace of judgment, that the bad may be consumed, and the good separated (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.29">Jr 6:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.30">30</reference>). <div eID="gen20650" type="x-p"/>
entries.007e62bc58cfd1fedb4e3c7383d4eb43ff1099d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11411"/><div sID="gen20651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11411"/>23. From this verse to the end he shows the general corruption of all ranks. <div eID="gen20651" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fdf0033a89708fc967f18e8206f158c0ca0f162: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11412"/><div sID="gen20652" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11412"/><hi type="bold">24. land ... not cleansed--</hi>not cleared or cultivated; all a scene of desolation; a fit emblem of the moral wilderness state of the people.<div eID="gen20652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor rained upon--</hi>a mark of divine "indignation"; as the early and latter rain, on which the productiveness of the land depended, was one of the great covenant blessings. Joel (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>) promises the return of the former and latter rain, with the restoration of God's favor. <div eID="gen20653" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fb5494f410ffd33a70f701411bc1b57a514d6c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11413"/><div sID="gen20654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11413"/><hi type="bold">25. conspiracy--</hi>The false prophets have conspired both to propagate error and to oppose the messages of God's servants. They are mentioned first, as their bad influence extended the widest.<div eID="gen20654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prey--</hi>Their aim was greed of gain, "treasure, and precious things" (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.9">Ho 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.3">Zep 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.14">Mt 23:14</reference>).<div eID="gen20655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made ... many widows--</hi>by occasioning, through false prophecies, the war with the Chaldeans in which the husbands fell. <div eID="gen20656" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5e50ac352dbc76af77a5e72c1537083983b2fe1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11414"/><div sID="gen20657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11414"/><hi type="bold">26. Her priests--</hi>whose "lips should have kept knowledge" (Mal 2:7).<div eID="gen20657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">violated--</hi>not simply transgressed; but, have done violence to the law, by wresting it to wrong ends, and putting wrong constructions on it.<div eID="gen20658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put no difference between the holy and profane, &c.--</hi>made no distinction between the clean and unclean (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.10">Le 10:10</reference>), the Sabbath and other days, sanctioning violations of that holy day. "Holy" means, what is dedicated to God; "profane," what is in common use; "unclean," what is forbidden to be eaten; "clean," what is lawful to be eaten.<div eID="gen20659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am profaned among them--</hi>They abuse My name to false or unjust purposes. <div eID="gen20660" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecd71086610fa121224043b2f220d6a0f7879477: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11415"/><div sID="gen20661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11415"/><hi type="bold">27. princes--</hi>who should have employed the influence of their position for the people's welfare, made "gain" their sole aim.<div eID="gen20661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wolves--</hi>notorious for fierce and ravening cruelty (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.2">Mi 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.9-Mic.3.11">3, 9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.12">Joh 10:12</reference>). <div eID="gen20662" type="x-p"/>
entries.97afabb32b25e168cf11b697011e10f331dff428: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11416"/><div sID="gen20663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11416"/>28. Referring to the false assurances of peace with which the prophets flattered the people, that they should not submit to the king of Babylon (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.10">Eze 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.29">Eze 21:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">Jr 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.16">23:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.9">27:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen20663" type="x-p"/>
entries.f981792420989e24783a317fc3c042dcec431293: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11417"/><div sID="gen20664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11417"/><hi type="bold">29. The people--</hi>put last, after the mention of those in office. Corruption had spread downwards through the whole community.<div eID="gen20664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrongfully--</hi>that is, "without cause," gratuitously, without the stranger proselyte giving any just provocation; nay, he of all others being one who ought to have been won to the worship of Jehovah by kindness, instead of being alienated by oppression; especially as the Israelites were commanded to remember that they themselves had been "strangers in Egypt" (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.21">Ex 22:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">23:9</reference>). <div eID="gen20665" type="x-p"/>
entries.f003b4ad0715c9ff00520a0d5f0e9ead8f0fb83d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11418"/><div sID="gen20666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11418"/><hi type="bold">30. the hedge--</hi>the wall (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.5">Eze 13:5</reference>); image for leading the people to repentance.<div eID="gen20666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20667" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the gap--</hi>the breach (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Psa 106:23</reference>); image for interceding between the people and God (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Ge 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.11">Ex 32:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.16.48">Nu 16:48</reference>).<div eID="gen20667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I found none--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.1">Jr 5:1</reference>)--not that literally there was not a righteous man in the city. For Jeremiah, Baruch, &c., were still there; but Jeremiah had been forbidden to pray for the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">Jr 11:14</reference>), as being doomed to wrath. None now, of the godly, knowing the desperate state of the people, and God's purpose as to them, was willing longer to interpose between God's wrath and them. And none "among them," that is, among those just enumerated as guilty of such sins (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.25-Ezek.22.29">Eze 22:25-29</reference>), was morally able for such an office. <div eID="gen20668" type="x-p"/>
entries.70cf616041c99b66ef5fc0f55db3e926abb7cbb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11419"/><div sID="gen20669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11419"/><hi type="bold">31. their own way ... recompensed upon their heads--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.10">Eze 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.21">11:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">16:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">Is 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.19">Jr 6:19</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.22"/>

entries.14c2d69df6217c4e5da23f971f3712dff62207bc: <div eID="gen31862" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31865" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains a recital of the sins of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Eze.22.1-Eze.22.12">Eze 22:1-12</reference>; for which God threatens it with severe judgments, <reference osisRef="Eze.22.13-Eze.22.16">Eze 22:13-16</reference>, in order to purify it from the dross, <reference osisRef="Eze.22.17-Eze.22.22">Eze 22:17-22</reference>. And as the corruption is general, pervading prophets, priests, princes, and people; so, it is declared, shall be the punishment, <reference osisRef="Eze.22.23-Eze.22.31">Eze 22:23-31</reference>.
entries.78c44f6f068f5cb4502147fa0f8439f2cc161a41: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31866" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou judge the bloody city - Pronounce the sentence of death against the murderers. <div eID="gen31866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31867" type="x-p"/> Show her all her abominations - And a most revolting and dreadful catalogue of these is in consequence exhibited.
entries.77398311b699f5884d901490030d743d1ee7c4ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31868" type="x-p"/> Her time may come - Till now, it was my long-suffering; she has fulfilled her days - completed the time of her probation; has not mended, but is daily worse; therefore her judgment can linger no longer.
entries.5d4f2fde0d384de70671132f3200349a3d2b8e30: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31869" type="x-p"/> Thou art become guilty in thy blood - Thou art guilty of blood.
entries.796979fdc839e375153ae6135d117b7399e3e96a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31870" type="x-p"/> Those that be near - Both distant as well as neighboring provinces consider thee the most abandoned of characters; and through thee many have been involved in distress and ruin.
entries.aade25e5b4843184a74d7c51b7ed7a7a8dff69bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31871" type="x-p"/> Behold, the princes - Ye are a vile and murderous people, and your princes have been of the same character. Like people, like prince.
entries.e2067e108f57073b20423f6886ac0f1dd3f993cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31872" type="x-p"/> In thee have they set light - The children do not reverence their parents. Parental affection and filial respect do not exist among you. The stranger is not only not succoured, but he is oppressed. The widows and fatherless are vexed by wrongs and exactions.
entries.0d62f338beb324e273443182faa9450274015472: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31873" type="x-p"/> Thou hast despised - All my ordinances are not only neglected, but treated with contempt; and my Sabbaths profaned. There is not only no power of godliness among you, but there is no form.
entries.d372ff6fbd9fd6ac7384c81d8e11f81a9df06b0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31874" type="x-p"/> In thee are men that carry tales - Witnesses that will swear any thing, even where life is concerned. <div eID="gen31874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31875" type="x-p"/> They eat upon the mountains - Sacrifice to idols, and celebrate their festivals.
entries.7205619a345519df066444970f83ea2aa03fcc1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31876" type="x-p"/> In thee have they discovered - They are guilty of the most abominable incest and unnatural lust. <div eID="gen31876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31877" type="x-p"/> On thee have they humbled - In their unholy and unnatural connexions, they have not abstained from those set apart because of their infirmities. The catalogue of crimes that follow is too plain to require comment.
entries.98581b651f67c1c715a51f7279c6def496f5581e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31878" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt know that I am the Lord - I shall so deal with and punish thee, that thou shalt be obliged to own the vindictive hand of a sin-avenging God.
entries.7769557d3aae81b35870f8ea25ba3db39bf06291: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31879" type="x-p"/> The house of Israel is to me become dross - They are all like base metal - brass, tin, iron, and lead alloyed together with silver. Ye must be put in the furnace, and subjected to the most intense fire, till your impurities are consumed away. No ordinary means will avail any thing; the most violent must be resorted to.
entries.331f88a393e4b3b1757c4a7684a2e995b8d52d47: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen31879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31880" type="x-p"/> I will gather you - Jerusalem is represented here as the fining pot; all the people are to be gathered together in it, and the Chaldean fire is to knelt the whole. And God will increase thy sufferings: as the refiner blows the fire with his bellows, so God will blow upon you with the fire of his wrath, <reference osisRef="Eze.22.21">Eze 22:21</reference>.
entries.6b4707d508d59426dacc1498c67d70a848e3344a: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen31880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31881" type="x-p"/> Thou art the land that is not cleansed - Thou art like a country where there is no rain, either to cleanse the garments, or fertilize the ground.
entries.6885f457155d786ea2ec81d8445f02a0127bc97c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen31881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31882" type="x-p"/> There is a conspiracy - The false prophets have united together to say and support the same things; and have been the cause of the destruction of souls, and the death of many, so that widows, through their means, are multiplied in thee.
entries.a604060ea10e29305efbdf25248bb172bb4c7e62: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen31882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31883" type="x-p"/> Her priests - Even they whose lips should preserve knowledge, have not instructed the people: they have violated my law, not only in their private conduct, but in their careless and corrupt manner of serving in my temple.
entries.561b0aa06fd554b5f1a2e6b34f932f70c6d1500a: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen31883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31884" type="x-p"/> Her princes - Are as bad as her priests; they are rapacious, and grievously oppress the people by unjust impositions in order to increase their revenues.
entries.0328d585fb9624651abbdc6c8dc44f8871adc2c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen31884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31885" type="x-p"/> Her prophets - Even those who profess themselves to be my prophets, have been unfaithful in the discharge of their office; have soothed the people in their sins, and pretended to have oracles of peace and safety when I had not spoken to them.
entries.78fdee3b0eddbc254bcc795c376d58aa4ae5d5af: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen31885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31886" type="x-p"/> The people - All that have power or authority have abused it; vexed and oppressed the poor, the needy, and the stranger.
entries.5b364c8cb0a6d3f6713144fdd8fedccf54af3bdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen31886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31887" type="x-p"/> I sought for a man - I saw that there was a grievous breach made in the moral state and feeling of the people, and I sought for a man that would stand in the gap; that would faithfully exhort, reprove and counsel with all long-suffering and doctrine. But none was to be found!
entries.f611d7dad7b19444164dd8977b4c2a045ad36dca: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen31887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31888" type="x-p"/> Therefore - Because of the profligacies already mentioned; because of the false worship so generally practiced; because of the false prophets tolerated; because of the unholy and profane priesthood; because of the oppressive princes; because of the unfaithful and deceiving prophets; because of the oppressions of petty officers; and because of the total corruption of manners in all ranks, places, offices, etc.: - <div eID="gen31888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31889" type="x-p"/> Have I poured out mine indignation - consumed them with the fire of my wrath - Considering the above, has there not been sufficient reason why I should abandon such a people, and pour out upon them such a destructive storm of calamities?  <chapter eID="Ezek.22"/> <div eID="gen31889" type="x-p"/>

entries.01c35624120a1f4281949a212fbdb7f5795b0f9c: <div sID="gen14983" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Ezek.22" sID="Ezek.22"/> <div eID="gen14983" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3df9358635e008e8c617471db9296bafbb9d4f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7"/><title type="x-s3">The Sins of Jerusalem and Israel</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7"/>Ezekiel 22:1-16 <div sID="gen14984" type="x-p"/> To the prediction of the judgment in Ezekiel 21 there is appended another description of the sins of Jerusalem and Israel, by which this judgment is occasioned. The chapter contains three words of God, which are connected together both in substance and design, viz., (1) The blood-guiltiness and idolatry of Jerusalem accelerate the coming of the days when the city will be an object of scorn to all the world (vv. 1-16); (2) The house of Israel has become dross, and is to be melted in the fire of tribulation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.17-Ezek.22.3">Eze 22:17-22); (3</reference>) All ranks of the kingdom - prophets, priests, princes, and people - are thoroughly corrupt, therefore has the judgment burst upon them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.23-Ezek.22.31">Eze 22:23-31</reference>). <div eID="gen14984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14985" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.1-Ezek.22.12">Eze 22:1-12</reference> <div eID="gen14985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14986" type="x-p"/> Blood-guiltiness of Jerusalem and the burden of its sins. <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.1-Ezek.22.5">Eze 22:1-5</reference> contain the principal accusation relating to bloodshed and idolatry; and <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.6-Ezek.22.16">Eze 22:6-16</reference> a further account of the sins of the people and their rulers, with a brief threatening of punishment. - Eze 22:1. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 22:2. <hi type="italic">And thou, son of man, wilt thou judge? wilt thou judge the city of blood-guiltiness? then show it all its abominations,</hi> Eze 22:3. <hi type="italic">And say, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, City, which sheddeth blood in the midst of it, that her time may come, and maketh idols within itself for defilement.</hi> Eze 22:4. <hi type="italic">Through thy blood which thou hast shed hast thou made thyself guilty, and through thine idols which thou hast made hast thou defiled thyself, and hast drawn thy days near, and hast come to thy years; therefore I make thee a scorn to the nations, and ridicule to all lands.</hi> Eze 22:5. <hi type="italic">Those near and those far off from thee shall ridicule thee as defiled in name, rich in confusion.</hi> - The expression 'התשׁפּט וגו proves this address to be a continuation of the reproof of Israel’s sins, which commenced in Eze 20:4. The epithet city of blood-guiltiness, as in Ezekiel <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.6">Eze 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.9">Eze 24:9</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.3.1">Nah 3:1</reference>), is explained in Eze 22:3. The apodosis commences with והודעתּהּ, and is continued in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.3">Eze 22:3</reference> (ואמרתּ). לבוא עתּהּ, that her time, i.e., her time of punishment, may come: עתּהּ, like יומו in Eze 21:30. ועשׂתּה is not a continuation of the infinitive לבוא, but of the participle שׁפכת. עליה, of which different renderings have been given, does not mean “over itself,” i.e., as a burden with which it has laden itself (Hävernick); still less “for itself” (Hitzig), a meaning which על never has, but literally “upon,” i.e., in itself, covering the city with it, as it were. ותּקריבי, thou hast brought near, brought on thy days, that is to say, the days of judgment, and hast come to, arrived at thy years, sc. the years of visitation and punishment (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.23">Jer 11:23</reference>). This meaning is readily supplied by the context. טמאת ה, defiled, unclean with regard to the name, i.e., having forfeited the name of a holy city through capital crimes and other sinful abominations. מהוּמה is internal confusion, both moral and religious, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Amo 3:9</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.10-Ps.55.12">Psa 55:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen14986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14987" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.6-Ezek.22.12">Eze 22:6-12</reference> there follows an enumeration of a multitude of sins which had been committed in Jerusalem. - Eze 22:6. <hi type="italic">Behold, the princes of Israel are every one, according to his arm, in thee to shed blood.</hi> Eze 22:7. <hi type="italic">Father and mother they despise in thee; toward the foreigner they act violently in the midst of thee; orphans and widows they oppress in thee.</hi> Eze 22:8. <hi type="italic">Thou despisest my holy things, and desecratest my Sabbaths.</hi> Eze 22:9. <hi type="italic">Slanderers are in thee to shed blood, and they eat upon the mountains in thee; they practise lewdness in thee.</hi> Eze 22:10. <hi type="italic">They uncover the father’s nakedness in thee; they ravish the defiled in her uncleanness in thee.</hi> Eze 22:11. <hi type="italic">They take gifts in thee to shed blood; interest and usury thou takest, and overreachest thy neighbours with violence, and thou forgettest me, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> - By the repetition of the refrain, to shed blood (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.6">Eze 22:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.9">Eze 22:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.12">Eze 22:12</reference>), the enumeration is divided into three groups of sins, which are placed in the category of blood-guiltiness by the fact that they are preceded by this sentence and the repetition of it after the form of a refrain. the first group (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.6-Ezek.22.8">Eze 22:6-8</reference>) embraces sins which are committed in daring opposition to all the laws of morality. By the princes of Israel we are to understand primarily the profligate kings, who caused innocent persons to be put to death, such, for example, as Jehoiakim (2Ki 24:4), Manasseh (2Ki 21:16), and others. The words אישׁ  are rendered by Hitzig and Kliefoth, they were ready to help one another; and in support of the rendering they appeal to Psa 83:9. But in that case אישׁ לזרעו would stand for לזרע אישׁ rof dnat, or rather for אישׁ זרוע לאישׁ, - a substitution which cannot be sustained. Nor can they be taken in the sense proposed by Hävernick, every one relying upon his arm, i.e., looking to physical force alone, but simply every one according to his arm, i.e., according to his strength or violence, are they in thee. In this case היוּ does not require anything to be supplied, any more than in the similar combination in Eze 22:9. Followed by למען with an infinitive, it means to be there with the intention of doing anything, or making an attempt, i.e., to direct his efforts to a certain end. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.7">Eze 22:7</reference> it is not the princes who are the subject, but the ungodly in general. הקלּוּ is the opposite of כּבּד (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.12">Exo 20:12</reference>). In the reproofs which follow, compare Exo 22:20.; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">Lev 19:13</reference>; Deu 24:14. With insolence and violence toward men there is associated contempt of all that is holy. For <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.22.8">Eze 22:8</reference></hi>, see Eze 20:13. - In the second group, <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.9-Ezek.22.11">Eze 22:9-11</reference>, in addition to slander and idolatry, the crimes of lewdness and incest are the principal sins for which the people are reproved; and here the allusion to Lev 18 and 19 is very obvious. The reproof of slander also points back to the prohibition in Lev 19:16. Slander to shed blood, refers to malicious charges and false testimony in a court of justice (vid., 1Ki 21:10-11). For eating upon the mountains, see Eze 18:6. The practice of <hi type="italic">zimmâh</hi> is more specifically described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.10">Eze 22:10</reference> and Eze 22:11. For the thing itself, compare <reference osisRef="Lev.18.7-Lev.18.8">Lev 18:7-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">Lev 19:15</reference> and Lev 19:9. The threefold אישׁ in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.11">Eze 22:11</reference> does not mean every one, but one, another, and the third, as the correlative רעהוּ shows. - The third group, <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.12">Eze 22:12</reference>, is composed of sins of covetousness. For the first clause, compare the prohibition in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.2">Exo 23:2</reference>; for the second, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.8">Eze 18:8</reference>, Eze 18:13. The reproof finishes with forgetfulness of God, which is closely allied to covetousness.
entries.cfc47e89ea23cc067010d42d1c0f278579e8df49: <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.17-Ezek.22.22">Eze 22:17-22</reference> <div eID="gen14988" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Refining of Israel in the Furnace of Besieged Jerusalem</title> <div sID="gen14989" type="x-p"/> Eze 22:17. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 22:18. <hi type="italic">Son of man, the house of Israel has become to me as dross; they are all brass, and tin, and iron, and lead in the furnace; dross of silver have they become.</hi> Eze 22:19. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Because ye have all become dross, therefore, behold, I gather you together in Jerusalem.</hi> Eze 22:20. <hi type="italic">As men gather together silver, and brass, and iron, and lead, and tin into the furnace, to blow the fire upon it for melting, so will I gather (you) together in my anger and my wrath, and put you in and melt you.</hi> Eze 22:21. <hi type="italic">And I will collect you together, and blow the fire of my wrath upon you, that ye may be melted therein.</hi> Eze 22:22. <hi type="italic">As silver is melted in the furnace, so shall ye be melted therein (viz., in Jerusalem), and shall learn that I Jehovah have poured out my wrath upon you.</hi> - This second word of God rests no doubt upon the figure in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.22.15">Eze 22:15</reference></hi>, of the uncleanness or dirt of sin; but it is not an exposition of the removal of the dirt, as predicted there. For that was to be effected through the dispersion of Israel among the nations, whereas the word of God, from <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.17">Eze 22:17</reference> onwards, represents the siege awaiting Jerusalem as a melting process, through which God will separate the silver ore contained in Israel from the baser metals mingled with it. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.18">Eze 22:18</reference> it commences with a description of the existing condition of Israel. It has turned to dross. היוּ is clearly a perfect, and is not to be taken as a prophetical future, as Kliefoth proposes. Such a rendering is not only precluded by the clause 'יען היות  in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.19">Eze 22:19</reference>, cut could only be made to yield an admissible sense by taking the middle clause of the verse, “all of them brass and tin,” etc., as a statement of what Israel had become, or as a preterite in opposition to all the rules of Hebrew syntax, inasmuch as this clause merely furnishes an explanation of היוּ־לסוּג. סוּג, which only occurs here, for סיג signifies dross, not smelting-ore (Kliefoth), literally, <hi type="italic">recedanea</hi>, the baser ingredients which are mixed with the silver, and separated from it by smelting. This is the meaning here, where it is directly afterwards interpreted as consisting of brass, tin, iron, and lead, and then still further defined as סגּים כּסף, dross of silver, i.e., brass, tin, iron, and lead, with a mixture of silver. Because Israel had turned into silver-dross of this kind, the Lord would gather it together in Jerusalem, to smelt it there as in a smelting furnace; just as men gather together brass, iron, lead, and tin in a furnace to smelt them, or rather to separate the silver contained thereon. קבצת כּסף, literally, a collection of silver, etc., for “like a collection.” The כ <hi type="italic">simil</hi>. is probably omitted for the sake of euphony, to avoid the discord occasioned by prefixing it to קבצת. Ezekiel mentions the silver as well, because there is some silver contained in the brass, iron, etc., or the dross is silver-dross. התּוּך, <hi type="italic">nomen verbale</hi>, from נתך in the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>, smelting; literally, as the smelting of silver takes place in the furnace. The smelting is treated here simply as a figurative representation of punishment, and consequently the result of the smelting, namely, the refining of the silver by the removal of the baser ingredients, is not referred to any further, as in the case in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.22">Isa 1:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.27-Jer.6.30">Jer 6:27-30</reference>; Mal 3:2-3. This smelting process was experienced by Israel in the last siege of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans.
entries.08f2d23416923fc8b2abf821b9e238ebdf0bad27: <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.23-Ezek.22.31">Eze 22:23-31</reference> <div eID="gen14989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14990" type="x-p"/> The corrupt state of all classes in the kingdom is the immediate cause of its destruction. - Eze 22:23. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 22:24. <hi type="italic">Son of man, say to it, Thou art a land which is not shined upon, nor rained upon in the day of anger.</hi> Eze 22:25. <hi type="italic">Conspiracy of its prophets is within it; like a roaring lion, which rends in pieces the prey, they devour souls, take possessions and money; they multiply its widows within it.</hi> Eze 22:26. <hi type="italic">Its priests violate my law and profane my holy things; they make no distinction between holy and unholy, and do not teach the difference between clean and unclean, and they hide their eyes from my Sabbaths, and I am profaned among them.</hi> Eze 22:27. <hi type="italic">Its princes in the midst of it are like wolves, which rend prey in pieces, that they may shed blood, destroy souls, to acquire gain. Eze 22:28. And its prophets plaster it with cement, seeing what is worthless, and diving lies for them, saying, “Thus saith the Lord Jehovah,” when Jehovah hath not spoken.</hi> Eze 22:29. <hi type="italic">The common people offer violence and commit theft; they crush the wretched and the poor, and oppress the foreigner against right.</hi> Eze 22:30. <hi type="italic">I seek among them for a man who might build a wall and step into the breach before me on behalf of the land, that I might not destroy it, but I find none.</hi> Eze 22:31. <hi type="italic">Therefore I pour out my anger upon them; I destroy them in the fire of my wrath, I give their way upon their head, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> - To show the necessity for the predicted judgment still more clearly, in the third word of God contained in this chapter a description is given of the spread of deep corruption among all classes of the people, and the impossibility of saving the kingdom is plainly shown. The words אמר־להּ, “say unto her,” are taken by most of the commentators as referring to Jerusalem, the abominations of which the prophet is commanded to declare. But although the clause, “thou art a land,” etc. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.24">Eze 22:24</reference>), could unquestionably be made to harmonize with this, yet the words of <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.30">Eze 22:30</reference>, “I sought for a man who might stand in the gap before Jehovah for the land,” indicate most unquestionably that this word of God is directed against the land of Judah, and consequently להּ must be taken as referring to ארץ which follows, the pronoun is this case being placed before the noun to which it refers, as in Num 24:17. Any allusion to the city of Jerusalem would therefore be somewhat out of place, inasmuch as in the preceding word of God the object referred to was not the city, but the house of Israel, or the nation generally, from which a transition is here made to the land, or the kingdom of Judah. The meaning of <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.24">Eze 22:24</reference> is a disputed question. לא מטהרה היא, which is rendered ἡ οὐ βρεχομένηin the Sept., is taken by most of the expositors to mean, “it is not cleansed,” the form מטהרה being correctly rendered as a participle <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> of טהר. But this rendering does not furnish any appropriate sense, unless the following words לא גּשׁמהּ are taken as a threat: there shall not be rain, or it shall not be rained upon in the day of wrath. But this view is hardly reconcilable with the form of the word. גּשׁמהּ, according to the Masoretic pointing with <hi type="italic">Mappik</hi> in the ה, is evidently meant to be taken as a noun גּשׁם = גּשׁם. In that case, if the words were intended to contain a threat, יהיה ought not to be omitted. But without a verb the words contain a statement in harmony with what precedes. We regard the <hi type="italic">Chetib</hi> גשׁמה as the perfect <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> גּשׁמהּ. And let it not be objected to this that the <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> of this verb is not met with elsewhere, for the form of the noun גּשׁם with the <hi type="italic">u</hi> sound does not occur anywhere else. As a perfect <hi type="italic">Pual</hi>, לא גּשׁמהּ is a simple continuation of the participial clause לא מטהרה היא, containing like this an affirmation, and cannot possibly be taken as a threat or prediction. But “not cleansed” and “not rained upon” do not agree together, as rain is not a means of purification according to the Hebrew idea. It is true that in the law the withdrawal or suspension of rain is threatened as a punishment from God, and the pouring out of rain is promised as a theocratical blessing. But even if the words are taken in a tropical sense, as denoting a withdrawal of the blessings of divine grace, they will not harmonize with the other clause, “not cleansed.” We therefore take מטהרה in the sense of “shined upon by the light,” or provided with brightness; a meaning which is sustained by <reference osisRef="Exod.24.10">Exo 24:10</reference>, where <hi type="italic">tohar</hi> occurs in the sense of splendour, and by the kindred word <hi type="italic">tzohar</hi>, light. In this way we obtain the suitable thought, land which has neither sunlight nor rain in the day of wrath, i.e., does not enjoy a single trace of the divine blessing, but is given up to the curse of barrenness. <div eID="gen14990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14991" type="x-p"/> The reason for this threat is given in Eze 22:25., where a picture is drawn of the moral corruption of all ranks; viz., of the prophets (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.25">Eze 22:25</reference>), the priests (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.26">Eze 22:26</reference>), the princes (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.27">Eze 22:27</reference>), and the common people (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.29">Eze 22:29</reference>). There is something very striking in the allusion to the prophets in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.25">Eze 22:25</reference>, not so much because they are mentioned again in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.28">Eze 22:28</reference>, - for this may be accounted for on the ground that in the latter passage they are simply introduced as false advisers of the princes, - as on account of the statement made concerning them in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.25">Eze 22:25</reference>, namely, that, like lions tearing their prey, they devour souls, etc.; a description which is not given either in Ezekiel 13 or elsewhere. Hitzig therefore proposes to alter נביאיה into נשׂיאיה, after the rendering ἀφηγούμενοι given by the lxx. This alteration of the text, which confines itself to a single letter, is rendered very plausible by the fact that almost the same is affirmed of the persons mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.25">Eze 22:25</reference> as of the princes in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.27">Eze 22:27</reference>, and that in the passage in Zephaniah (Zep 3:3-4), which is so similar to the one before us, that Ezekiel appears to have had it in his mind, the princes (שׂריה) and the judges (שׁפטיה) are called the prophets and the priests. The נשׂיאים here would correspond to the שׂרים of Zephaniah, and the שׂרים to the שׁפטים. According to <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.6">Eze 22:6</reference>, the נשׂיאים would indicate primarily the members of the royal family, possibly including the chief officers of the crown; and the שׂרים eht dna ;n (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.27">Eze 22:27</reference>) would be the heads of tribes, of families, and of fathers’ houses, in whose hands the national administration of justice principally lay (cf. Exo 18:19.; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.13-Deut.1.18">Deu 1:13-18</reference>; and my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol</hi>. ii. §149). I therefore prefer this conjecture, or correction, to the Masoretic reading, although the latter is supported by ancient witnesses, such as the Chaldee with its rendering ספרהא, scribes, and the version of Jerome. For the statement which the verse contains is not applicable to prophets, and the best explanation given of the Masoretic text - namely, that by Michaelis, “they have made a compact with one another as to what kind of teaching they would or would not give; and in order that their authority may continue undisturbed, they persecute even to blood those who do not act with them, or obey them, but rather contradict” - does not do justice to the words, but weakens their sense. קשׁר is not a predicate to 'נב, “they are (i.e., form) a conspiracy;” but 'נב  is a genitive. At the same time, there is no necessity to take קשׁר in the sense of “company,” a rendering which cannot be sustained. The fact that in what follows, where the comparison to lions is introduced, the נביאים (נשׂיאים) are the subject, simply proves that in the first clause also these men actually form the prominent idea. There is no ground for supplying המּה to 'כּארי  (they are like, etc.); but the simile is to be linked on to the following clause. נפשׁ אכלוּ is to be explained from the comparison to a lion, which devours the prey that it has captured in its blood, in which is the soul, or <hi type="italic">nephesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen 9:4</reference>; Lev 17:11.). The thought is this: in their insatiable greed for riches they sacrifice men and put them to death, and thereby multiply the number of victims (for the fact, see <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.5">Eze 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.7">Eze 19:7</reference>). What is stated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.26">Eze 22:26</reference> concerning the priests is simply a further expansion of Zep 3:4, where the first two clauses occur word for word; for קדשׁ in Zephaniah is really equivalent to קדשׁי, holy things and deeds. The desecration of the holy things consisted in the fact that they made no distinction between sacred and profane, clean and unclean. For the fact, compare <reference osisRef="Lev.10.10">Lev 10:10</reference>-11. Their covering their eyes from the Sabbaths showed itself in their permitting the Sabbaths to be desecrated by the people, without offering any opposition (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.27">Jer 17:27</reference>). <div eID="gen14991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14992" type="x-p"/> The comparison of the rulers (<hi type="italic">sārim</hi>) to ravening wolves is taken from Zep 3:3. Destroying souls to acquire gain is perfectly applicable to unjust judges, inasmuch as, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.18.21">Exo 18:21</reference>, the judges were to hate בּצע. All that is affirmed in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.28">Eze 22:28</reference> of the conduct of the false prophets is repeated for the most part <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> from <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.10">Eze 13:10</reference>,<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.9">Eze 13:9</reference>, and Eze 13:7. By להם, which points back to the three classes of men already mentioned, and not merely to the <hi type="italic">sārim</hi>, the prophets are represented as helpers of those who support the ungodly in their wicked ways, by oracles which assured them of prosperity. עם  (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.29">Eze 22:29</reference>), as distinguished from the spiritual and secular rulers of the nation, signifies the common people. With reference to their sins and wickednesses, see <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.7">Eze 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.12">Eze 18:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.18">Eze 18:18</reference>; and for the command against oppressing the poor and foreigners, compare <reference osisRef="Exod.22.20-Exod.22.21">Exo 22:20-21</reference>; Deu 24:17. - The corruption is so universal, that not a man is to be found who could enter into the gap as a righteous man, or avert the judgment of destruction by his intercession. מהם refers not merely to the prophets, who did not enter into the gap according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.5">Eze 13:5</reference>, but to all the classes previously mentioned. At the same time, it does not follow from this, that entering into the gap by means of intercession cannot be the thing intended, as Hitzig supposes. The expression לפני בּעד הארץ clearly refers to intercession. This is apparent from the simple fact that, as Hitzig himself observes, the intercession of Abraham for Sodom (Gen 18:13.) was floating before the mind of Ezekiel, since the concluding words of the verse contain an obvious allusion to Gen 18:28. Because the Lord does not find a single righteous man, who might intercede for the land, He pours out His anger upon it, to destroy the inhabitants thereof. With reference to the fact and the separate words employed, compare Ezekiel 21:36; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.4">Eze 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.10">Eze 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.21">Eze 11:21</reference>, and Eze 16:43. It does not follow from the word ואשׁפּך, that Ezekiel “is speaking after the catastrophe” (Hitzig). For although ואשׁפּך expresses the consequence of Jehovah’s seeking a righteous man and not finding one, it by no means follows from the occurrence of the preterite ולא מצאתי that ואשׁפּך is also a preterite. ואשׁפּך is simply connected with ואבקּשׁ as a consequence; and in both verbs the <hi type="italic">Vav consec.</hi> expresses the sequence of thought, and not of time. The seeking, therefore, with the result of not having found, cannot be understood in a chronological sense, i.e., as an event belonging to the past, for the simple reason that the preceding words do not record the chronological order of events. It merely depicts the existing moral condition of the people, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.30">Eze 22:30</reference> sums up the result of the description in the thought that there was no one to be found who could enter in the gap before God. Consequently we cannot determine from the imperfect with <hi type="italic">Vav consec.</hi> either the time of the seeking and not finding, or that of the pouring out of the wrath.  <chapter eID="Ezek.22"/> <div eID="gen14992" type="x-p"/>
